newsitem.title: JAPAN: Land market languor chokes Japan recovery-analysts.
newsitem.headline: Land market languor chokes Japan recovery-analysts.

text.p: A stagnant land market is at the heart of Japan's economic woes, and unless the government faces up to the problem it will keep choking off the economy's weak recovery, analysts say.
"The Japanese economy is a slave to land," said Shoji Kitta, managing director of Tokyo Tanshi Co Ltd, Japan's largest money broker.
"A lack of land liquidity is at the core of the nation's bad loan problem, not just for the ailing banking sector but for a broad range of corporate Japan," he said.
But politicians and heads of banks and real estate firms are afraid to call for moves to boost the liquidity of land as it could mean a chaotic nosedive in property prices, analysts said.

"Even if the government put in place some measures to raise the liquidity, market forces will not allow land prices to recover easily," said Teruhiko Mano, an adviser to the president of Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi Ltd.

"Japan has only two options...either allow a quick, steep fall in land prices and deal with its destructive impact on the economy, or let land prices fall only mildly and put up with a long-lasting drag on the economy," he said.
Real estate values in Japan have declined since the economic "bubble" of inflated asset prices burst in the early 1990s. But analysts said land prices are still too high to attract buyers.

But any further falls in land values would exacerbate the bad loan problems hanging over the banks, which have extensive real estate holdings as collateral, while hurting general contractors and real estate companies, they said.
"Unless land transactions are revitalised by changing the tax system on land holdings and transactions, a healthy economic recovery is unlikely to be achieved," Kitta said.
Also, Japanese banks, obsessed by bad loan write-offs, are wary of providing fresh loans to finance property purchases.

The Ministry of Finance said non-performing assets at Japanese banks alone totalled 29 trillion yen ($250 billion) at the end of September. Most were related to loans to real estate firms or backed by land as collateral.
Unless land prices fall steeply to the point where investors can expect good returns, no one will put money into property, Mano said.
Some analysts said Japan has refused shock therapy for its land-related ills for too long, and as a result the economy is still stuck in neutral despite fiscal and monetary stimuluses.

Japan slashed its discount rate, which the central bank charges on overnight loans to commercial banks, to a record low 0.5 percent in September 1995, but the government is still forecasting growth of only 1.9 percent in real gross domestic product for the fiscal year starting on April 1.
"Both Japanese stocks and land will have to trim more fat to narrow the price gaps with overseas markets," Mano added.
The price earnings ratio of Japan's main share index, the Nikkei 225, is over 60, against around 20 in the U.S. It is calculated by dividing share prices by earnings per share.
Due to the land-related bad loan problems, banks and real estate shares were among the hardest-hit sectors during recent tumbles in Tokyo share prices.
So far, Japanese bureaucrats have looked for painless solutions to the problem but have not offered any answers.
An influential government panel last November called for a fundamental change in land policies, but failed to make specific proposals on the current tax system on land holdings.
